passages.title: The Moon Catcher
passages.text: Long ago, before people measured months by calendars, the moon was said to travel close enough for mountain goats to brush it with their horns. Villagers in the valley depended on the moon's light to guide their planting, fishing, and travel. When the moon was full, they worked late into the evening. When it was thin, they rested and waited. In one village lived Nalin, a young net maker who was admired for his clever fingers. His nets never tore, and his knots held through storms. At first, Nalin used his skill to help the village. He repaired fishing nets, built hammocks for children, and taught others how to twist strong rope. Soon, praise began to change him. Nalin decided that ordinary work was beneath him. "If I can catch fish and birds," he boasted, "then I can catch the moon itself." The elders warned him that the moon belonged to everyone and should not be trapped for one person's glory, but Nalin laughed at their concern. On the night of the harvest moon, Nalin climbed the tallest cedar and cast his finest net into the sky. To everyone's astonishment, the glowing moon tangled in the net and stopped moving. At first, the valley cheered. The night became bright as noon, and Nalin bowed as if he had created the light himself. But the days that followed grew strange. Tides weakened. Birds lost their direction. Farmers could not judge the proper planting time. Children became restless because night no longer felt like night. The villagers begged Nalin to release the moon, but he refused until his own shadow disappeared beneath the endless silver light. Finally, Nalin understood that a gift shared by all should not be controlled by one person's pride. He climbed the cedar and cut the net. The moon rose higher than ever before, too distant for any net to reach. From that night on, people remembered Nalin whenever moonlight touched a rope or knot, and they taught their children that talent becomes dangerous when it forgets responsibility.

choices.B: Natural cycles matter only when people use them for farming and travel.
choices.C: A person who receives praise may become more helpful to the community.
choices.D: Using a gift selfishly can harm others and turn talent into a source of danger.

sections.title: The Green Belt Movement / Planting Day

passages.title: The Green Belt Movement
passages.text: In the 1970s, many communities in Kenya faced problems connected to deforestation. Trees had been cleared for farms, fuel, and development. Without enough trees, soil washed away more easily, streams dried up, and families had to walk farther to find firewood and clean water. Wangari Maathai, a Kenyan scientist and activist, believed that planting trees could address several problems at once. In 1977, she helped begin the Green Belt Movement. The movement encouraged women to plant tree seedlings in their communities. Planting trees was practical, but it was also political because it gave ordinary citizens a way to improve the land and speak up about decisions affecting their lives. The work was not easy. Some leaders criticized Maathai and tried to silence the movement. Still, communities continued planting. Over time, the Green Belt Movement helped plant millions of trees and brought attention to the connection between the environment, democracy, and community responsibility. Maathai later became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Her work showed that environmental action can also be a form of civic action when it helps people protect their homes, resources, and voices.

passages.title: Planting Day
passages.text: Amina carried the seedling in both hands because its roots were wrapped in newspaper and hope. The hill above her village looked tired. Rain had carved brown lines through the soil, and the stream where her grandmother once washed clothes had thinned to a thread. "Hold it straight," Mama said, kneeling beside the small hole. Amina pressed the seedling into place while her mother pushed dark soil around it. Around them, other women worked in pairs. Some laughed as they planted; others wiped sweat from their faces and kept digging. A truck passed on the road below, carrying logs toward the city. Amina looked from the logs to the fragile tree in her hands. It seemed impossible that something so small could answer something so large. Mama seemed to read her thoughts. "A tree is not only wood," she said. "It is shade. It is soil staying where it belongs. It is water waiting in the ground." She touched Amina's wrist gently. "And today, it is our answer." Years later, Amina would walk the same hill and stand beneath branches that had once fit in her palms. She would remember that planting had not felt like a speech or a protest. It had felt like work. Only later did she understand that work can become a voice when enough hands repeat it.

passages.title: Letter to the Principal
passages.text:
Dear Principal Ahmed,

One issue affecting many students at Crestview Middle School is limited access to the library after school. Currently, the library closes at 3:15 p.m., only fifteen minutes after dismissal. I am writing to ask that the library remain open until 4:30 p.m. at least three days each week.

Some people may argue that most students can complete research or homework at home. However, that assumes every student has a quiet place to work, reliable internet, or someone available to help with sources. The school library already provides these supports during the day, so extending access would help students who need them most.

Longer library hours would also support academic programs. Students in debate club, science fair, and advanced reading groups often need books, databases, and a calm workspace. Last month, our media specialist reported that more than forty students asked to use the library after dismissal but had to leave because it was closing.

It is true that keeping the library open longer may require scheduling an adult supervisor. Still, the school could begin with a small pilot program. For example, the library could stay open on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays during the months when major projects are assigned. Afterward, the school could review attendance data and decide whether the program should continue.

The library should be more than a room students pass during the day. It should be a place where students can continue learning when the final bell rings. I encourage the school to test extended library hours so that more students have access to the resources they need.

Sincerely,
Marisol Chen

questions.prompt: What claim does Marisol make in the letter?

choices.A: Students should be required to join debate club, science fair, or advanced reading groups.
choices.B: The school should keep the library open until 4:30 p.m. at least three days each week.
choices.C: The media specialist should stop tracking how many students visit the library.
choices.D: Homework should be completed only during the school day.

questions.prompt: What does the word pilot mean as it is used in paragraph 4?
questions.stimulus: Still, the school could begin with a small pilot program.

choices.A: A temporary trial used to test whether a larger plan should continue
choices.B: A person responsible for guiding a vehicle or aircraft safely
choices.C: A school rule that becomes permanent as soon as it is announced
choices.D: A student activity completed independently without adult supervision

choices.B: The library shelves were painted blue over the summer to make the room feel calmer.
choices.C: Many students say the library is a comfortable place to talk with friends after school.
choices.D: A sign near the entrance reminds students to return books before checking out new ones.

passages.title: Urban Heat Islands
passages.text: During a science unit on cities and climate, students learned about urban heat islands. An urban heat island is an area of a city that becomes warmer than nearby rural areas. Dark pavement, rooftops, traffic, and fewer trees can cause cities to absorb and hold more heat. The teacher introduced the word mitigation and explained that it means reducing the severity or harmful effects of a problem. Students studied several mitigation strategies, including planting trees, using lighter-colored roofing materials, and designing shaded public spaces.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does mitigation mean?

choices.A: The process of measuring the temperature of rural areas
choices.B: A method for increasing traffic in crowded city streets
choices.C: A way of reducing the harmful effects of a problem
choices.D: The study of how buildings are arranged in a city

passages.title: Encyclopedia Entry
passages.text: Coral reefs are underwater ecosystems built by tiny animals called coral polyps. Reefs provide habitat for many marine species and help protect coastlines from waves. In recent decades, warming ocean temperatures, pollution, and physical damage have harmed reefs around the world. Scientists and local groups now use restoration methods such as growing coral fragments in nurseries and attaching them to damaged reefs.

passages.title: Field Report
passages.text: During a reef restoration project near the Florida Keys, divers placed nursery-grown coral fragments onto a damaged reef. The team recorded water temperature, coral survival, and the number of fish returning to the area. After six months, several fragments had attached successfully, and small fish were observed sheltering among the new coral growth. Researchers cautioned that restoration helps, but reducing pollution and warming remains necessary.

questions.prompt: A student took notes from both sources. Which note correctly paraphrases information from both sources?

choices.A: Coral reefs support ocean life and protect coasts; restoration teams may grow coral fragments before placing them on damaged reefs.
choices.B: Coral nurseries are used mostly to attract fish back to reefs after storms move rocks underwater.
choices.C: Restoration has ended the danger of warming seas because most coral fragments survive the first six months.
choices.D: Pollution can help damaged reefs recover when divers attach new coral fragments near returning fish.

passages.title: Argumentative Essay Draft
passages.text:
Some people think the city should build protected bike lanes near schools. Protected bike lanes create a space between riders and cars, which can make students feel safer traveling to school. If more students are able to bike, traffic near school entrances may also decrease. This could reduce delays for buses and families during morning arrival.

Opponents may argue that adding bike lanes would remove some parking spaces. That concern matters, but the city could begin with streets that already have extra curb space. The city could also collect traffic data during a trial period before making permanent changes.

Overall, protected bike lanes would give students another safe transportation option while helping reduce congestion around schools.

passages.title: Student Paragraph
passages.text: Our class visited the history museum last Friday. We saw a display about ancient trade routes. We also watched a short film about how goods, languages, and ideas moved between regions. The trip helped me understand that trade can shape culture as well as economics.

questions.stimulus: We saw a display about ancient trade routes. We also watched a short film about how goods, languages, and ideas moved between regions.

passages.title: Narrative Draft
passages.text: When I volunteered at the animal shelter, I expected to spend the afternoon filling water bowls and sweeping floors. Instead, the director handed me a nervous gray dog named Pepper and asked me to sit with her until she calmed down. At first, Pepper trembled whenever anyone walked past the kennel. I spoke softly and kept my hand still near the gate. After several minutes, she stepped closer. By the end of the afternoon, she rested her chin on my shoe. The next week, a family came to meet Pepper. I watched her walk toward them with her tail low but wagging. When the youngest child sat on the floor, Pepper gently placed her head in the child's lap.

questions.prompt: Which sentence would best conclude the narrative by reflecting on the experience?

choices.A: That day taught me that patience can make space for trust to grow.
choices.B: After we finished, I helped refill the water bowls and sweep near the kennels.
choices.C: Pepper's gray fur, small silver tag, and quiet steps made her easy to recognize.
choices.D: Animal shelters often depend on volunteers during weekends, summers, and school breaks.

passages.title: Narrative Passage
passages.text: Malik had promised to perform his poem at the community center, but the storm arrived an hour before the event. Rain hammered the windows, and thunder shook the hallway lights. Malik folded his poem into his pocket and told himself that no one would come anyway. When he reached the center, only a few chairs were filled. His voice felt trapped behind his teeth. Then his grandmother, still wearing her raincoat, took a seat in the front row and nodded once. Malik stepped to the microphone. At first, his words came out thin and quick. Halfway through the poem, he looked up and saw people leaning forward. He slowed down. By the final line, his voice was steady enough to reach the back wall.

Character change shown through Malik's voice becoming steadier
Dialogue between Malik and his grandmother about the poem
A flashback explaining when Malik first began writing poetry
A prediction that the microphone will stop working during the poem

sections.title: Greek and Latin Roots and Affixes

passages.title: Science Vocabulary
passages.text: During science class, students learned vocabulary used to describe light and life. The teacher explained that photosynthesis contains the Greek root photo, meaning light, and synthesis, meaning putting together. Students also examined words such as microscope, biodegradable, aquatic, and invisible to see how roots and affixes can help readers determine meaning.

questions.prompt: Based on your knowledge of Greek and Latin roots and affixes, which TWO explanations are accurate? Select TWO.

choices.A: Photosynthesis relates to using light to put materials together.
choices.B: Microscope means a tool used to study very small things.
choices.C: Biodegradable means unable to break down through natural processes.
choices.D: Aquatic means related to air or flight.
choices.E: Invisible means able to be seen clearly without help.
